summary: Specifies the MD4 message digest algorithm, designed by Ron Rivest, which turns a message of any length into a short fixed-size fingerprint. It is informational, not a standard, and was replaced by RFC 1320.

eli5.summary: It is a machine that squishes any message into a tiny fingerprint. If the message changes even a little, the fingerprint looks different.

subtitle: A fast 128-bit cryptographic message digest algorithm for signing and checksums.

tldr.problem: Digital signatures and data integrity checks require a way to compress a large file into a small fixed-size fingerprint that can be signed with RSA, and this must be fast on contemporary hardware.
tldr.mechanism: MD4 takes a message of arbitrary length and computes a 128-bit message digest (fingerprint) by padding the input, processing it in 16-word blocks through three rounds of operations using bitwise functions, and outputting four 32-bit words.
tldr.outcome: MD4 became widely used for digital signatures and integrity checking but was later found to have cryptographic weaknesses and was replaced by MD5 (RFC 1320), which is also now considered broken.

today: RFC 1186 is an Informational RFC from October 1990 that has been obsoleted by RFC 1320 (MD5). MD4 is now considered cryptographically broken and should not be used for security purposes. It survives in some legacy systems and as a component in NTLM authentication schemes, but all new systems should use modern cryptographic hash functions like SHA-256 or SHA-3.

sections.title: Why Message Digests Matter
sections.content:
A message digest (also called a hash or fingerprint) is a small fixed-size number computed from a message of any length such that:

  • Different messages almost always produce different digests (collision resistance)
  • It is computationally infeasible to find any two messages with the same digest
  • It is computationally infeasible to find a message with a pre-specified target digest

Message digests are essential for digital signature schemes where a large file must be compressed before being signed with RSA public-key cryptography. Instead of signing the entire file (which would be slow), you sign the small digest, and anyone can verify the signature matches.

MD4 was designed by Ron Rivest to be fast on 32-bit machines: it ran at approximately 1.45 million bytes per second on a SUN Sparc workstation, 70,000 bytes per second on a DEC MicroVax II, and 32,000 bytes per second on a 20MHz 80286 processor.
sections.eli5: A message digest turns any document into a short code. If you change even one word, the code changes completely. You can sign the code instead of the whole document, and that proves you wrote the document. MD4 was fast enough to use with very big files.

sections.title: How MD4 Works
sections.content:
MD4 processes a message in five steps:

Step 1: Padding. The message is padded so that its length (in bits) is congruent to 448, modulo 512. A single "1" bit is appended, followed by zero bits, ensuring the result is exactly 64 bits short of a multiple of 512 bits.

Step 2: Append length. A 64-bit representation of the original message length is appended, making the total length a multiple of 512 bits (or 16 words of 32 bits each).

Step 3: Initialize buffer. Four 32-bit registers (A, B, C, D) are initialized to constant values: A = 0x67452301, B = 0xefcdab89, C = 0x98badcfe, D = 0x10325476.

Step 4: Process blocks. The message is processed as 16-word blocks. For each block, three rounds of operations are performed. Each round uses a different bitwise function (f, g, h) applied to the registers with left-rotate shifts and message word inputs. Specific magic constants derived from the square roots of 2 and 3 are used in rounds 2 and 3.

Step 5: Output. After processing all blocks, the final values of A, B, C, D form the 128-bit message digest.
sections.eli5: MD4 chops the message into pieces, mixes them through three rounds of bit-twiddling, and outputs a tiny fingerprint. The same message always gives the same fingerprint, but changing one bit makes a completely different fingerprint.

sections.title: Design and Extension
sections.content:
MD4 does not require large substitution tables and can be implemented compactly. The algorithm's auxiliary functions are mathematically interesting: function f is a bitwise conditional (if-then-else), function g acts as a majority function (outputting 1 if at least two of three inputs are 1), and function h is the bitwise XOR (parity) function. When the input bits are independent and unbiased, the output bits remain independent and unbiased.

The RFC includes an option for obtaining 256-bit output by running two copies of MD4 in parallel with modified initial states and magic constants representing the cube roots of 2 and 3. The A register values are exchanged after every 16-word block in the two copies.

The document includes a complete reference implementation in C with detailed comments on endianness (byte ordering) considerations, macros for the core operations, and sample output.
sections.eli5: MD4 is designed to be simple and fast, with no giant lookup tables. You can also run two MD4 machines in parallel and glue their results together if you need a bigger fingerprint.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC documents security properties at the time of publication. It conjectures that finding two messages with the same digest requires on the order of 2^64 operations (the birthday attack bound for a 128-bit digest), and finding any message with a pre-specified digest requires on the order of 2^128 operations. The RFC states that MD4 should be sufficient for implementing very high-security hybrid digital signature schemes with RSA.

However, the RFC acknowledges that it is "a relatively new algorithm and further security analysis is of course justified." Subsequent cryptanalysis revealed significant weaknesses: collisions were found in MD4 within years, and the algorithm is now considered cryptographically broken. MD4 was replaced by MD5 and then by more secure algorithms such as SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3. Modern systems should not use MD4 or MD5 for cryptographic purposes.
sections.eli5: When MD4 was created, people thought it was impossible to break. But mathematicians found tricks to forge the fingerprint, so it turned out the machine had a secret back door. Now we use better fingerprint machines.
